neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Dysarthria — nasal quality speech. Dysphagia to solids and liquids; coughing on thin liquids. Bilateral palatal weakness. No facial weakness. No ophthalmoplegia.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral upper extremity weakness: shoulder abduction 3/5, elbow flexion 3+/5, grip 4/5. Lower extremity strength 4+/5 bilaterally. Able to walk.
neurological_exam.sensory: Sensation intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration in all extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent bilateral biceps and brachioradialis. Trace patellar and Achilles bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin intact. No cerebellar signs.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 2.8 L (predicted 4.2 L — 67%). NIF: -34 cmH2O. Low-grade fever 37.7°C on admission two days ago, now resolved. Bulbar involvement predominant with relative leg sparing — atypical distribution.

patient.chief_complaint: Five-day progressive dysphagia and arm weakness with nasal speech, no preceding infection recalled, gait preserved.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. D. is a 32-year-old graphic designer presenting with a 5-day history of progressive oropharyngeal and upper extremity weakness. He initially noticed mild difficulty swallowing solid food approximately 5 days ago, which has progressed to coughing on thin liquids. Two days ago, he developed bilateral arm weakness making it difficult to lift objects overhead or type at his workstation. He recalls a low-grade fever with mild malaise approximately 10 days prior that he attributed to fatigue and resolved spontaneously without medical attention. He denies any bloody diarrhea or respiratory illness. He has no diplopia, no ptosis, and no lower extremity weakness — notably, he was able to walk into the emergency department unassisted and his gait appears normal. His speech has a nasal quality and he cannot clear his throat effectively. He has no sensory deficits. His partner noted that he had been having trouble buttoning his shirt for the past 3 days. He denies any prior neurological symptoms, and there is no family history of neuromuscular disease. There is no honey exposure, no wound, no tick exposure, and no canned food ingestion that would suggest botulism. The descending pattern with predominant bulbar and arm involvement — with preserved leg strength and absent upper extremity reflexes — is atypical and raises a challenging diagnostic question.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: PCB variant — upper extremity demyelination with leg sparing

optimal_actions.action: NPO and NGT placement — aspiration risk

critical_actions: Recognize PCB variant — descending pattern with bulbar/arm predominance is GBS, not botulism or MG
NPO status and NGT — severe dysphagia with aspiration risk
Serial FVC/NIF — bulbar GBS has high intubation risk even when FVC above threshold
Anti-GT1a antibody is the serological marker for PCB GBS variant
contraindicated_actions: Discharging without monitoring — bulbar GBS can decompensate rapidly
key_reasoning_points: Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial GBS is a regional variant with descending pattern: bulbar > arms > legs; legs may be completely spared
Anti-GT1a IgG is the key serological marker for PCB variant (distinct from anti-GQ1b in Miller Fisher)
PCB variant can be missed when classic ascending pattern is expected — preserved leg strength and gait do NOT exclude GBS
Absent upper extremity reflexes with normal lower extremity reflexes reflects the regional demyelination distribution
Bulbar dysfunction in GBS carries high aspiration and intubation risk independent of FVC — proactive airway management is critical

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: PCB GBS variant spares the legs — preserved leg strength does not exclude GBS
